Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:7: And whoever is able to learn Torah and does not learn it, of him the verse says (Jeremiah 2:5), "thus says the LORD: what wrong did your fathers find in Me, that they distanced themselves from Me and went after emptiness and became empty?"
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:8: One who washes his shoes and goes out to the marketplace is among the haughty of spirit; one whose chin is turned to the side, whose hat is tilted backward, whose sandal straps are one on top of the other, and who holds the straps of his tefillin in his hand, twirling them as he walks in the marketplace, is among the haughty of spirit. All the haughty of spirit resemble idolatry, as it is said (Deuteronomy 7:26), "and do not bring an abomination into your house," and elsewhere it says (Proverbs 16:5), "an abomination to the LORD is every proud heart" — "abomination" is said here and "abomination" there: just as the "abomination" said here is idolatry, so the "abomination" said there is idolatry. It is said elsewhere (Deuteronomy 13:14), "worthless men have gone out," and it is said elsewhere (2 Samuel 23:6), "and the worthless are all like thorns thrust away" — but one who walks in His ways is blessed, as it is said (Psalms 103:20), "bless the LORD, His angels, mighty in strength, who do His word." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:9: Further, to complete the acquisition of the attribute of humility, one must distance himself from envy, desire, and honor, which drive a person from this world and the World to Come (4:21), and the pious Rabbi Yosef Yavetz, peace be upon him, elaborated on this at length; especially envy, which is a branch of anger.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:10: It is written in the book Beit Middot, found among us in manuscript, several matters on the disgrace of the quality of envy (Gate of Envy). I saw fit to copy his words since they pertain to practical life. These are his words: the quality of envy is a branch of anger, and no person escapes it, for we see that all people are drawn each after his fellow — for when a person sees his fellow acquire worldly matters, whether kinds of food, or clothes, or building a house, or gathering wealth, then he strains to attain the same, thinking, my friend has this, I too shall have such a thing. This is what King Solomon, peace be upon him, alluded to in saying (Ecclesiastes 4:4), "I saw that all labor and all skill in work come from a man's envy of his neighbor."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:11: Whoever is overcome by this quality is disgraceful, for this envy brings him to covetousness — for when a person does not take to heart and envies what his fellow has, he then covets, and the Torah says (Exodus 20:14), "you shall not covet." And when he covets, he then robs, as it is written (Micah 2:2), "and they covet fields and rob them." A person overcome by covetousness comes close to transgressing the Ten Commandments — for there was a story of a man who had a wicked neighbor, with a wall separating between them, and the wicked one coveted the man's wife and some of his possessions. One Friday he heard the man tell his wife, "today I wish to go out on a business trip," and so he did. What did that wicked man do? He went that Sabbath night and broke through the wall separating them, transgressing "remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy"; he went and raped the woman he coveted and lay with her, transgressing "you shall not commit adultery"; and then he began to steal the money — she cried out and he stood over her and killed her, transgressing "you shall not murder"; and when he stole and robbed what he coveted, he transgressed "you shall not steal" and "you shall not covet." The next day his father and mother came and rebuked him; he arose and struck them, transgressing "honor your father and your mother." Afterward he was brought before the court and testified together with his worthless companion that those items he took were his own pledge, having been pledged to him by the woman's husband — transgressing "you shall not bear [false witness]." In the end the matter was revealed and became known, and his wickedness became known, and out of shame he went to bad company and denied the living God, transgressing "I am [the LORD your God]." And in the end he became devoted to idolatry, transgressing "you shall have no [other gods]" and "you shall not bow down to them nor serve them" — and all this was caused by the portion of covetousness; we find, then, that the coveter comes close to transgressing the whole Torah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:12: There is another way, closer to observation, of how envy and covetousness corrupt a person, and regarding this King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 23:17), "let your heart not envy sinners, but [be zealous] in the fear of the LORD all day." When a person envies sinners, seeing their wealth and success, and sees the righteous disparaged and afflicted with sufferings, his soul thereby grows disgusted with God's judgments and statutes, and he despises those who study and fulfill Torah — as it is said in Malachi (3:13-15), "your words have been harsh against Me... you have said, it is vain to serve God, and what profit is it that we have kept His charge and walked mournfully before the LORD of Hosts? So now we call the arrogant fortunate; indeed, evildoers prosper; indeed, they test God and escape." This matter brings foolishness into people's understanding and turns their hearts backward, upon seeing a wicked man for whom it is good and a righteous man for whom it is bad, and through this they walk in the stubbornness of their hearts and say, "so-and-so did such and such and he is wealthy and successful, so let us do the same, and whatever happens to him will happen to us too" — and all this comes from the cause of envy of the wicked and covetousness of their wealth and ease, and therefore they cast off the yoke of the commandments.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:13: But the righteous do not envy the wicked nor covet their money or their ease, for they think that their wealth is kept for their harm, and their ease will destroy them, compared to the great good hidden for the righteous; and they think that the poverty and pressure of the righteous is to refine and purify them and increase their merit for the World to Come. There is no doubt that one who thinks this way will not covet or envy, but will rejoice upon seeing the ease of the wicked, and say, if this is so for those who anger Him, how much more so for those who do His will — He gives and gives again.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:14: Envy comes from a deficiency of the soul — if he envies a person's beauty, might, or wealth, he thereby shows he does not desire what the Name, blessed be He, decreed for him, and this is like a servant who complains about his master's deeds and is not reconciled to his own affairs; such is not a faithful servant — how much more so should one not complain against the Creator, blessed be He, all of whose deeds are upright and wise, that no one should question Him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:15: Whoever envies comes to strife, as you find with Korach, who envied the honor of Elizaphan ben Uzziel, and through this he, the nursing infants, and their company were lost from the world.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:16: Envy among people is like an illness to the body, and it brings on consumption. The sage said to his son, beware of envy, for it is recognizable in you, since your face changes from the evil of your heart, and that person you envy rejoices at the distress of your heart — why should you make your enemies rejoice, that they take revenge and rejoice over you?
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:17: The envious person robs his own soul, for he mourns continually and his mind is diminished from the great envy hidden within him, and his heart has no room to study, to pray with intent, and to do good deeds. Every person finds a sweet taste except the envious one, for he does not taste a sweet taste in his food until his fellow's good fortune reverses.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:18: For every hatred there is hope — for if he hates his fellow because he robbed him, once the robbed item is returned to him, he will remove the hatred from his heart; and likewise every hatred that depends on some matter, once that matter is corrected for you, the hatred will be nullified from his heart — except for one who hates his fellow out of envy. The sage said, do not envy your fellow for what he has, for he will enjoy it while you will be filled with worry, grief, distress, and trouble. And the sage said, the coveter and the envious were created only for anger.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:19: The sages of Israel used to pray, "let not our envy be upon others, nor the envy of others upon us" (Yerushalmi Berachot 4:2). Why did they pray regarding this quality more than the other qualities? The matter is thus: many people cause others to envy them when they wear fine clothes, causing others to envy them — therefore they used to pray, since they might be causing envy in others thereby; and the Torah says (Leviticus 19:14), "and do not place a stumbling block before the blind." Therefore it is a good quality for a person not to wear excessively fine and praiseworthy clothes, neither he, nor his wife, nor his household, and likewise regarding foods and other matters, so that others do not envy him. Also, whoever the Holy One, blessed be He, has granted wealth and possessions should be generous to the rich and the poor and conduct himself gently with them and do kindness with them — we have already elaborated on how to be beloved by everyone — then they will not envy him nor covet what is his. But it is fitting for a person to rise in good qualities that are his glory, and let others envy him and covet to become like him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:20: Whoever is careful not to envy, his body does not waste away and the worm does not rule over him, as it is written (Proverbs 14:30), "and envy is the rot of the bones" — meaning, whoever has envy, his bones decay. Likewise a person should distance himself from envy and covetousness, and not covet anything that is in others' possession, and should not say, "I covet my fellow's item, and I will give him money for that item" if his intent is to sell — for then it is forbidden to pressure him, since he would be embarrassed to refuse him empty-handed, and thus it would be coercion. All the more so if the one who covets is honored, such that if he asks for something, the other's face would not fall [in refusal] — it is forbidden for him to ask for what is his, or to take it to show that he desires it, and he should not demand that matter unless he knows his fellow will give it to him with a willing soul.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:21: A parable of the coveter and the envious: they walked together on the road and met a king. The king said to them, one of you shall ask something of me, and it shall be given to him, and double to his fellow. The coveter desired double the portion, and the envious one did not want to ask first, since he would envy if double were given to his fellow. In the end the coveter pressured the envious one to ask first, so the envious one asked that one of his own eyes be gouged out, and both of his fellow's.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:22: See how much evil depends on envy — for the primordial serpent envied Adam and brought death to the world, and of it a curse is said (Genesis 3:14), "upon your belly shall you go, and dust shall you eat." See what happened to Cain, to Korach, to Balaam, to Achitofel, to Gehazi, to Adonijah, to Absalom, and to Uzziah, who set their eyes on what was not fitting for them — and it was not enough that they were not given what they sought, but even what was already in their possession was taken from them. From all these a person should learn and be careful of envy and covetousness, and think that even what is in his possession is not truly his, for tomorrow he may pass on and it will be gone, and of what use is it to him that it is not truly his? Regarding this it is said (Proverbs 27:1), "for you do not know what a day may bring forth."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:23: A great reward belongs to one who is careful about envy and covetousness — for most transgressions, if a person transgresses them and is embarrassed, he abandons them because of the shame; thus the reward for this comes from restraining himself from envy and covetousness. For one who refrains from robbery and theft is afraid lest it become known and revealed and he be caught, embarrassed, and suffer great loss.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:24: But envy and covetousness are hidden in the heart, concealed from people's eyes, so that no one can discern whether he is covetous or envious, since this matter is entrusted to the heart alone; and if he restrains himself from them, of him the verse says (Leviticus 19:14), "and you shall fear your God."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:25: Although envy is very evil, there is a place where it is very good, being one of the qualities of the supernal beings — when a person directs his envy toward the fear of the Name, as it is said (Proverbs 23:17), "let your heart not envy sinners, but [be zealous] in the fear of the LORD all day." Regarding this the Sages said (Bava Batra 21a), the envy of scribes increases wisdom — if a person sees another studying, envy takes hold in his heart and he says, this one studies all day, I too shall do so; and likewise regarding all other commandments and good qualities, each envies his fellow and grasps his fellow's good deeds. And if he sees a wicked person who has two or three good qualities, he should envy him regarding these and do them too.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:26: But one who envies his fellow who is occupied with Torah, commandments, and good deeds, and does not envy him thinking "this one does good deeds, so shall I too," but rather thinks in his heart and envies him because he has qualities greater than his own, and devises stratagems to nullify him and confuse him away from his Torah and his good deeds — this envy is a bad illness, sinning and causing others to sin, and he is a partner of Jeroboam ben Nevat.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:27: A person should always honor those who fear Heaven, students of Torah, and observers of commandments, and lend them a hand, and assist them with his body, his money, and all his ability — and then others will envy him and think, "we too shall do so, and we will be honored and helped as well" — and out of [motives] not for their own sake, one comes to [act] for their own sake.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:28: Were it not for envy, the world would not endure, for then no one would plant a vineyard, no one would marry, and no one would build a house, since all these matters come about because one person envies his fellow. One who builds a house should take to heart that he does so [partly from this motive], and likewise regarding a wife, each envying his fellow.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:29: Since the world depends on envy, one should direct all envy toward the sake of Heaven — if he builds a house, let him build within it a room for studying Torah, and let his house be a meeting place for the wise, and for bringing in guests and doing kindness for people, for had Abraham not envied, he would not have acquired heaven and earth. And when did he envy? When he asked Malkitzedek, "how did you come out of the ark?" He said to him, "through the charity we performed there." He said to him, "but what did you have in the ark to do charity with — were there poor people there? Were there not only Noah and his sons — with whom did you do charity?" He said to him, "with the animals, beasts, and birds, for we did not sleep but gave them their food." At that moment Abraham said to him, "had you not done charity with animals, beasts, and birds, you would not have come out of the ark; and if I do charity with people, created in the image of God, how much more so [should I be rewarded]!" At that moment, "and he planted an eshel [tamarisk] in Beersheba" — [an acronym for] *eating, *drinking, *escorting. For this a person should increase envy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:30: Also, a person should envy sinners and the wicked in order to fight against them and rebuke them, as our Sages of blessed memory said (Sanhedrin 81b), one who has relations with an Aramean woman, zealots may attack him. Moses was zealous against the Egyptian, as it is said (Exodus 2:12), "and he struck the Egyptian." And we likewise find Elijah (1 Kings 19:10), "I have been very zealous for the LORD, the God of Hosts, for the children of Israel have forsaken Your covenant." And it is likewise said of Pinchas (Numbers 25:11), "in his being zealous with My zeal among them," and the Name gave him his reward for this, as it is said, "therefore say, behold, I give him My covenant of peace." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:31: Further, to complete the attribute of humility, a person must conduct himself according to the conditions Torah scholars follow, as Rambam, peace be upon him, wrote in chapter 5 of Hilchot De'ot.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:32: Regarding the conditions of a Torah scholar, they explained in tractate Berachot (43b), these are their words: our Rabbis taught, six things are a disgrace for a Torah scholar: he should not go out perfumed into the marketplace; he should not go out alone at night; he should not go out with patched shoes; he should not converse with a woman in the marketplace; he should not recline at a gathering of the unlearned; and he should not be the last to enter the study hall. Some say, he should not take large strides, and he should not walk with an erect posture. Thus far their words. For each of these they explained a reason there in the Gemara, but we shall not copy all his words to avoid excessive length.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:33: The one more relevant to the matter of pride is "he should not walk with an erect posture," and they explained there that Rabbi Yehuda said, whoever walks with an erect posture, even four cubits, is as though he pushes against the feet of the Shechinah, as it is written (Isaiah 6:3), "the whole earth is full of His glory." Thus far his words. The reason is that he thereby becomes proud and shows that he has no master ruling over him, for it is the way of a servant to walk with humility and a bowed head before his master. And all his other matters, in his dress and his speech, he should conduct according to the conditions Rambam, peace be upon him, explained there, and he will certainly be complete in the attribute of humility in its generalities and particulars.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:34: When a person strives regarding the attribute of humility in all its particulars written in this Gate, he will find that included in the acquisition of the attribute of humility is the acquisition of all good qualities, and included in the attribute of pride is the totality of all disgraceful qualities — this is like the matter, "there is nothing higher than Oneg and nothing lower than Nega" (cf. Sefer Yetzirah 2:7); and it has already been explained that the proud person is afflicted with tzara'at, since one of the reasons afflictions come is haughtiness of spirit, and it is written (Leviticus 14:56), "and for a rising and a scab" — thus one who lacks humility lacks the good qualities. This is likewise explained in the beraita of tractate Kallah (ch. 3), these are his words: be like the lowest threshold of the house — this house, if it lacks a threshold, appears deficient, as though ruined; so too you need humility, and even if you are complete in all other qualities, if you lack humility, you are deficient — for so people say, "what a great man so-and-so would be were it not for his pride!" — to teach you thus: rather, "he who fears God shall come forth out of them all" (Ecclesiastes 7:18). Rava said, just as the threshold aligns the doors for closing and opening, so humility is a fence for wisdom. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:35: Regarding the merit of humility, there are many further merits besides those we explained in chapter 3. Further, they said in Sotah (5b): Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said, how great are the humble of spirit! For when the Temple stood, one who offered a burnt offering received the reward of a burnt offering, one who offered a meal offering received the reward of a meal offering; but one whose mind is lowly, the verse considers it as though he had offered all the sacrifices — and moreover, his prayer is not despised, as it is said (Psalms 51:19), "a broken and crushed heart, O God, You will not despise." And Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said, whoever sets his ways in this world merits to see the salvation of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said (ibid. 50:23), "and to one who sets his way I will show the salvation of God" — do not read "vesam" [and sets] but "vesham" [and there].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:36: Also in the World to Come his merit is great, as they expounded in Megillah (15b) on the verse (Isaiah 28:5), "on that day the LORD of Hosts shall be a crown of glory": Rabbi Elazar said in the name of Rabbi Chanina, the Holy One, blessed be He, is destined to be a crown on the head of every single righteous person, etc. — and they said, might one think for everyone [without qualification]? The verse teaches, "for the remnant of His people" — for one who makes himself like ownerless property [humble].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:37: Further, so that you recognize how many merits are in humility, I saw fit to copy the words of Menorat HaMaor of Rabbi Yisrael, of blessed memory, who elaborated at length on its merits. These are his words: great is humility, for which Abraham our father, peace be upon him, was praised — because the great men of his generation exalted him and called him "my lord," as it is said (Genesis 23:6), "hear us, my lord" — yet he, peace be upon him, lowered himself among them and submitted before them and conducted himself with the quality of humility and modesty, even with the lowly, as it is said (ibid. 23:12), "and Abraham bowed down" etc. And although he was a prophet, a prince, mighty, and wealthy, he was modest and humble and did not consider himself anything, saying (ibid. 18:27), "and I am but dust and ashes." A prophet — as it is written (ibid. 20:7), "return the man's wife, for he is a prophet." A prince — as it is written (ibid. 23:6), "you are a prince of God among us." Mighty — as it is written (ibid. 14:15), "and he divided himself against them by night, he and his servants, and struck them." Wealthy — as it is written (ibid. 13:2), "and Abram was very heavy with livestock" etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:38: Great is humility, for which Isaac our father, peace be upon him, was praised — for Avimelech expelled him from his kingdom, and he was successful in all his deeds and all his ways, as it is said (Genesis 26:12), "and Isaac sowed" etc., and because of his great wealth the Philistines envied him, as it is said (ibid. 26:14), "and he had possessions of flocks" etc. "and the Philistines envied him" etc. — and when Avimelech came to him, he did not repay him according to his deeds, but out of his great humility received him with a pleasant countenance and fed and gave drink to him and his men, as it is said (ibid. 26:30), "and he made them a feast" etc. "and Isaac sent them away" etc. This is among the qualities of humility and piety — not to repay one who did evil according to his evil, but to repay him good for evil.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:39: Great is humility, for which Jacob our father, peace be upon him, was praised — for out of his humility he conducted himself with honor toward his brother Esau, because Esau had come out into the air of the world a mere moment before him, and his messenger would say to him (Genesis 32:5), "thus says your servant Jacob" — not that he feared him lest he kill or be killed. Rabbi, when he wrote to Antoninus, would write "the utterance of your servant Judah," saying, "I am not better than my ancestors" (Bereshit Rabbah 75:5).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:40: Great is humility, for which Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, was praised, as it is said (Numbers 12:3), "and the man Moses was very humble." Why does it say "more than all men"? Rather, humble, and did not take pride in any of the qualities that people are accustomed to take pride in, such as kingship, prophecy, and wisdom — and although he had all the good qualities in the world, his heart was not proud in any of them, not even one. When he was in Egypt, although he was like the grandson of Pharaoh, he was distressed with Israel and bore their burdens with them; even when he was in the greatness of Heaven, he did not abandon his humility, as it is said (Exodus 17:12), "and they took a stone and placed it beneath him, and he sat on it" — did Moses not have a cushion or pillow to sit on? Rather, Moses said, Israel is in distress, so I too shall be in distress with them. And even at the time of the rebellion he did not abandon his humility, as it is said (Numbers 16:25), "and Moses arose and went to Datan and Aviram" — he did not become proud and say, "they are disputing with the Holy One, blessed be He, and shall I, like a king, go after them?" but in all his matters he was humble. Likewise you find that when Eldad and Medad prophesied, Joshua said to him (ibid. 11:28), "my lord Moses, restrain them" — what did he say to him? "Are you zealous for my sake? Would that even the servants and maidservants be prophets, and you seek that only I be a prophet? I, who requested these seventy elders," as it is said (ibid. 11:14), "I cannot bear it alone." Moreover, from the start he was fleeing from leadership, as it is said (Exodus 4:13), "send, please, by the hand of whomever You will send." Likewise, because of his humility, he did not look at the Shechinah in the thornbush, as it is said (Exodus 3:6), "and Moses hid his face," and he received reward as our Sages of blessed memory explained (Berachot 7a) — as reward for "and Moses hid his face," he merited a radiant countenance. Therefore, when the Holy One, blessed be He, praised him, He praised him only for the quality of humility, as it is said, "and the man Moses was very humble" — it does not say "wise" or "pious," only "humble."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:41: Great is humility, for which Aaron, peace be upon him, was praised — for the world's custom is that a person honors his household with worn-out garments etc., as we copied in the Gate of Awe, chapter 15; and so too Elazar the priest, the Levites, and the sons of Kehat were praised for it, as we wrote there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:42: Great is humility, by which Samuel the prophet, peace be upon him, was made great — for the angel called him three times, and he thought Eli was calling him, and was startled and awakened from his sleep to come to him three times, as it is said (1 Samuel 3:8), "and the LORD called Samuel again a third time" — and he was not proud, saying, "how long will this one keep calling me and I run to him?" And had he been [too proud to rise and] stayed asleep, he would have lost this great prophecy. Moreover, he traveled from place to place for Israel's needs but not for his own, as it is said (1 Samuel 7:16), "and he would go from year to year" etc. Moreover, when Israel said to him, "give us a king to judge us" (1 Samuel 8:6), he did not say to them, "behold, I am already like a king over you, and you seek a king?"
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:43: Great is humility, by which Saul was made great — when Samuel said to him (1 Samuel 9:20), "and to whom belongs all the desire of Israel? Is it not to you?" out of his humility he made himself small and said to him (ibid. 9:21), "am I not a Benjaminite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel, and my family the least" etc.? And at the time they sought to anoint him king, he went and hid himself among the baggage until they cast lots, as it is said (ibid. 10:22), "and the LORD said, behold, he is hidden among the baggage."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:44: Rabbi Yannai says, the verse explains thirteen good qualities in King Saul, peace be upon him. First, humble — "am I not a Benjaminite" etc. Second, that he heard his own disgrace and was silent, as it is said (1 Samuel 10:27), "and worthless men said, how shall this one save us?" etc., "but he was as one who kept silent" — as one who did not know. Third, that he forgave his own affront, as it is said (ibid. 11:12), "who is it that said, shall Saul reign over us? Bring the men, that we may put them to death," and it is written, "and Saul said, no man shall be put to death today." Fourth, that he was careful about the commandment of tzitzit, as it is said (1 Samuel 24:4 [24:5]), "and David arose and cut off the corner of Saul's robe secretly" — this "corner" is the tzitzit, as it is said (Numbers 15:38), "and they shall put upon the tzitzit of the corner." Fifth, that he would provide dowries for all the daughters of Israel who had no dowry of their own, as it is said (2 Samuel 1:24), "daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you in scarlet with luxuries, who put ornaments of gold upon your garments." Sixth, that he had the strength to repent — for although Samuel told him twice, "I will not return with you" (1 Samuel 15:26), he would say to him, "please forgive my sin and return with me, that I may bow before the LORD." Seventh, that he was modest, as it is said (1 Samuel 24:3), "and he came to the sheepfolds by the road, and there was a cave, and Saul went in to relieve himself" — "two folds and a cave" — and even so he covered himself, and because of that modesty he was saved from an unnatural death, as we learn in tractate Berachot (62b): and it says, "and to kill you, but I had compassion on you" (1 Samuel 24:10) — it should say "and I said," why "and I had compassion"? Rabbi Elazar said, David said to Saul, by the law of the Torah I am permitted to kill you — why? You are pursuing me, and one who comes to kill you, rise early and kill him first — but your modesty had compassion on you. What modesty was in Saul? As it is said, "and he came to the sheepfolds by the road" etc. — it was taught, a fold within a fold, and a cave within a cave; "to relieve himself" — Rabbi Elazar said, he covered himself like a sukkah. Eighth, that he spent his own money and was concerned for the money of Israel, as it is said (1 Samuel 11:7), "and the spirit of God prospered upon Saul when he heard" etc. "and he took a yoke of oxen and cut them in pieces" [distributing them at his own cost rather than the people's]. Ninth, that he ate ordinary food in a state of purity, as it is said (1 Samuel 20:26), "and Saul said nothing that day, for he thought, something has happened to him, he is impure, surely he is not pure" — to teach you that had it been a "mikreh" [chance impurity, i.e., nocturnal emission], he would not have come to his table [even then]. Tenth, that he sanctified consecrated items, as it is said (1 Chronicles 26:28), "and all that Samuel the seer, and Saul the son of Kish" had consecrated. Eleventh, that he equated his own honor with that of his servant, as it is said (1 Samuel 20:25), "and the king sat upon his seat as at other times, upon a seat by the wall" etc. [treating regular seating without special elevation]. Twelfth, that he was easily appeased — you find that when David appeased him in the cave, he was immediately appeased, as it is said (1 Samuel 26:21), "and Saul said, I have sinned; return, my son David." Thirteenth, that he knew David was destined to reign and sought his help, as it is said (1 Samuel 24:20), "and now, behold, I know that you shall surely be king, and the kingdom of Israel shall be established in your hand" etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:45: Great is humility, through which David was made great, as it is said (1 Chronicles 17:16-17), "and King David came and sat before the LORD and said, who am I" etc., and it is written, "and You have regarded me as a man of high degree" etc. He said to Him, Master of the universe, what am I, that You have compared me to Jacob our father, peace be upon him, who is engraved on the Throne, the image of man engraved above? And likewise Israel ask (Jeremiah 14:21), "do not disgrace the throne of Your glory" — that very form engraved on the Throne. And from where do we learn that He compared him to the Patriarchs? As it is said (2 Samuel 7:9), "and I will make you a name like the name of the great ones who are on the earth." Yet although he had all these qualities and all this honor, and was the anointed of the God of Jacob, and the sweet singer of Israel, and praised for several qualities, skilled in playing, mighty in war, a man of battle, understanding in speech, etc. (1 Samuel 16:18), and killed the lion and the bear in the field, and killed Goliath the Philistine, was son-in-law to the king, obedient and honored in his house, and he saved Israel from the hand of the Philistines — after all this, he was lowly in his own eyes and humble, and said to Saul when he pursued him (1 Samuel 24:15), "after whom has the king of Israel come out, after whom do you pursue — after a dead dog, after one flea" etc. And after all this honor, he ruled over Israel and Judah and conquered several kingdoms, and yet said (Psalms 22:7), "but I am a worm and not a man" etc.; and when he brought up the Ark of God from the house of Oved-Edom the Gittite to the city of David, he danced etc., as we elaborated in the final chapter of the Gate of Awe.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:46: Great is humility, for which Mordechai was praised — for at first he was fifth on the Sanhedrin, as it is said (Ezra 2:2), "who came with Zerubbabel, Yeshua, Nechemiah, Seraiah, Re'elaiah, Mordechai"; and once he became second to the king, it was not enough that he did not wish to be fourth, but even fifth in his own place he did not wish to be — but although his greatness increased, he lowered himself and made himself sixth, as it is said (Nehemiah 7:7), "those who came with Zerubbabel, Yeshua, Nechemiah, Azariah, Ra'amiah, Nachamani, Mordechai."
